name: (E)-Nerolidol

pubchem.title: Nerolidol
pubchem.description: Nerolidol is a farnesane sesquiterpenoid that is dodeca-1,6,10-triene which carries methyl groups at positions 3, 7 and 11 and a hydroxy group at position 3. It is a natural product that is present in various flowers and plants with a floral odor. Chemically, it exists in two geometric isomers, trans and cis forms. It is widely used in cosmetics (e.g. shampoos and perfumes), in non-cosmetic products (e.g. detergents and cleansers) and also as a food flavoring agent. It has a role as an antioxidant, a herbicide, an insect attractant, a pheromone, a volatile oil component, a flavouring agent, an antihypertensive agent, an antifungal agent, a neuroprotective agent, a cosmetic and an anti-inflammatory agent. It is a volatile organic compound, a tertiary allylic alcohol and a farnesane sesquiterpenoid.

consumer_summary.what_it_is: (E)-Nerolidol is a volatile sesquiterpenoid—a type of aromatic molecule—prized for its distinct floral scent. It is widely used as a flavoring agent in foods and a fragrance in perfumes, shampoos, and cleansers. In nature, it acts as a signaling molecule and pheromone, helping plants communicate and defend themselves against environmental stressors.
consumer_summary.found_in: It is notably found in tea leaves (Camellia sinensis), where its production is triggered by stress during manufacturing. It is also present in a wide variety of aromatic plants, including yarrow (Achillea millefolium), wild ginger (Zingiber zerumbet), and various Croton species.
consumer_summary.why_researchers_care: Researchers are drawn to (E)-nerolidol because of its diverse biological roles, ranging from plant defense to potential human health benefits. The scientific literature, which peaks at human observational research (Oxford level 2b), frequently explores its capacity to act as an antioxidant, an antimicrobial, and an anti-inflammatory agent. Scientists are particularly interested in how this floral compound interacts with cellular enzymes and receptors, exploring whether its protective effects in plants might translate into therapeutic uses for humans.

hypothesized_benefits.hypothesis: Researchers are exploring whether (E)-nerolidol's interactions with cellular pathways might support healthy cell cycles and tissue growth.
hypothesized_benefits.study_to_test_it: A randomized, placebo-controlled human clinical trial measuring specific cellular proliferation biomarkers over six months of supplementation.

hypothesized_benefits.hypothesis: If this bears out, (E)-nerolidol could be utilized to help manage systemic inflammation by interacting with enzymes like 15-lipoxygenase.
hypothesized_benefits.study_to_test_it: A randomized, double-blind human trial supplementing (E)-nerolidol and tracking inflammatory markers like CRP and 15-lipoxygenase activity over 12 weeks.

hypothesized_benefits.hypothesis: Scientists are curious if this plant defense molecule could be harnessed to support human immune responses against fungal or bacterial challenges.
hypothesized_benefits.study_to_test_it: A randomized controlled trial applying a topical (E)-nerolidol formulation to localized skin flora, measuring microbial counts and skin health over a four-week period.

hypothesized_benefits.hypothesis: Early animal work points toward a potential analgesic effect, raising the question of whether it could soothe discomfort in humans.
hypothesized_benefits.study_to_test_it: A phase 1/2 human clinical trial assessing subjective pain scores and safety profiles in healthy volunteers exposed to a standardized mild pain stimulus after receiving (E)-nerolidol.

consumer_summary.evidence_at_a_glance: Best evidence so far is human observational work (Oxford 2b) focusing on its antimicrobial and antioxidant properties; the remainder of the research consists of animal models and laboratory studies.
